item.title: Anticipating the End of Time
item.dc:creator: Jeri E. Wieringa
item.description:
A Historical Analysis through Topic Modeling

“We are living in the closing scenes of this earth’s history. Prophecy is fast fulfilling. The hours of probation are fast passing. We have no time – not a moment – to loose.”
Ellen White. Testimonies for the Church, Volume 8, 19041

Early Seventh-day Adventists were a people between times. Born out of the belief that William Miller had correctly identified 1844 as the year revealed in the books of Daniel and Revelations, this group of Protestant Christians understood themselves to be living in the last days, preparing for the rapidly approaching “second advent” of Jesus. Millennial expectation, however, is a difficult state to maintain.2 Although Seventh-day Adventists determined early on that predicting new dates for the second coming was no longer viable, at various period throughout their early history they understood themselves to be at the brink of the second coming. As the second coming continued to be delayed, their interpretations of the events since 1844 shifted, as did the emphasis they placed on different religious beliefs and practices. As a result, their theology and religious cultural was shaped by “Jesus’ nonappearance rather than his imminent reappearance,” as the most productive periods of development tended to occur in efforts to explain the why of the continuation of normal time.3

These periods correspond with but also offer an additional perspective on some of the standard narratives around religious revivals and the development of religious groups. Using the a 250 topic model of the periodical literature of the denomination, this study offers an extended examination of the cycles of expectation and explanation that mark the early development of the Seventh-day Adventist denomination. Using topics that capture Seventh-day Adventist language about end times as indicators of high periods of expectation, I argue that the religious group experienced four major cycles of expectation and adjustment between 1849 and 1920. In each cycle, the markers of the anticipated second coming shift and in the wake of anticipation, new emphases emerged that shifted the focus of the denomination increasingly outward. This framework also provides another way to understand Ellen White’s writings regarding gender and religious leadership, as she repeatedly embeds women’s labor within the central concerns of the current temporal imaginary.

This introduction to the study establishes the historical and theoretical frameworks, as well as methodology, and then uses the topic model to argue that there were four major cycles of end-times expectation during the first seventy years of the denomination. Each of these cycles is analyzed in the subsequent sections of the case study.

Introduction to Study

The revivals and millennial movements of the nineteenth century have been a frequent object of analysis for scholars of religion and American culture as transformative events that contributed to the “democratization of American culture”, the development of a “Christian” culture, the flourishing of social reform efforts, and the embrace of capitalism.4 William Miller’s 1843 and 1844 predictions feature in these standard narratives as an example of the lengths reached in the religious revivals of the early nineteenth century and of the flourishing of lay leaders and extra-denominational movements.5 Framed in term of the responses to individuals to the economic and social upheavals of the early years of the American republic, these studies focus on commonalities across American religious movements at particular points in time, tying general religious movement to broader cultural shifts and development. Since the 1970s, growing attention has been paid to the role of women in these religious revivals of the nineteenth century. Foundational to this effort is Catherine Brekus’ Strangers and Pilgrims, which traces the contributions of female preachers and visionaries to the religious movements of the first and second great awakenings.6

With increased attention to questions of gender, race, and class, scholars who examine patterns across multiple revivals have drawn attention to the ways women and members of other marginalized groups feature prominently during periods of upheaval or revival. Such analysis has been done using the frameworks of theorists such as Mary Douglas, Victor Turner, and Max Weber, parsing revival periods as moments of disruption in social norms and hierarchies, where members reject or challenge existing rituals until a new equilibrium is achieved and order is re-established.7 While these frameworks link the source of religious revivalism primarily to forces external to religious movements - such as economic or cultural disruption - they help explain periods of unusually expansive behavior within religious and cultural groups, as well as the more subtle but lasting cultural shifts that revival moments leave in their wake.8

As one of a small handful of examples in US religious history of a denomination led by a woman prophet, gender features frequently in the analysis of early Seventh-day Adventism. This treatment ranges from the personal history and role of Ellen White to analyses of the different role available to women at different points in the denomination’s history and the denominational culture itself as gendered feminine. With her prophetic career starting when she was just [] years old, scholarly analysis of Ellen White’s youth and her background in the Methodist church situates her well within the framework of a religious “rebel” - as someone whose religious commitments push the boundaries of existing ritual.9 At the point of White’s death in 1915, Seventh-day Adventism had progressed from a group at the edges of the Millerite movement to an established denomination, and one that was increasingly inscribing a gendered hierarchy based on “separate spheres” and female domesticity.10 Scholars have effectively used the Weber’s theory of “religion of the non-priviledged classes” (that it is “characterized by a tendency to allot equality to women”11) and the framework of “church” (or “denomination”) and “sect” to explain the Seventh-day Adventist trajectory from a religious group clearly on the edges of and critical toward their surrounding culture to an increasingly stable and overall respectable member of American Protestantism.12

These general patterns of accommodation and secularization - in the sense of becoming “like the world” - help explain the overall structural shifts in the Seventh-day Adventist theology and religious culture, but also obscure the ways that culture was negotiated at multiple point along the way. While Vance and Butler convincingly argue that trajectory of the Seventh-day Adventist denomination has historically been toward accommodation to prevailing cultural norms and toward increased affiliation with the traditional Protestant denomination, the early years of the sect indicate that this progression was complex and contested. As Vance notes with regard to Ellen White’s positions on female leadership in the denomination, “the seeming contradictions of White’s admonitions, life, and advice are not easily reconciled.”13

In this study, I use topic modeling to explore the seeming contradictions and changing emphases of the first seventy years of the denomination in light of two, I argue, related influences on Adventist thought: belief in the second coming and constructions of gender and ideas regarding female authority. First, I proceed from the assumption that early Adventist writers truly did believe themselves to be living at the edge of the second coming, that their experiences of the world were shaped by reference to a shortened temporal horizon or temporal imaginary. While their sense of time lengthens and the theological particulars change over time, the development of Seventh-day Adventism was critically shaped by their commitment to the Jesus’ imminent second coming, a belief felt at different times more acutely that others. Second, I posit that those periods of heightened expectation trigger periods of disruption, or “religious anti-ritualism,” when power structures and religious commitments are re-examined, both in the midst of expectation and in the realignments that follow as time persists.14 Through these cycles, as I show through this case study, the “world” to be reached with the Adventist message slowly widens and the understanding of that message expands. Due in large part to Ellen White’s continued leadership within the movement and through the upheavals brought on by periods of end-times expectation, at each turn and reformulation of the Adventist message, the religious life is gendered for both men and women in ways at odds with prevailing cultural norms. While these role are also circumscribed and influenced by broader cultural constructions, the result is a religious culture where women are consistently central to the work of salvation, and the overall culture, while patriarchal, also contains markable “feminine” characteristics.

Methodology

One of the ongoing challenges for scholarship that brings together methods from multiple disciplines is articulating how the information derived through methods typically foreign to humanities practice meaningfully contributes to the process of meaning-making. As argued by Tanya Clement, the linking of theory and methods is crucial to the process of situating the intellectual work of interdisciplinary scholarship.15 As part of bridging that gap, here I outline my interpretive strategy for moving from the topic model, a statistical representation of language patterns, to an argument for overall patterns in the denominational corpus.16 The full model, which you can engage via the model browser, parses the language of the denomination into 250 clusters of words that tend to co-occur on the pages of the periodicals.

Topic modeling, as I discuss in the project overview, is a form of computational analysis that has been used in humanities context for descriptions of a collection of documents and for document discovery, but of which are fewer clear examples of use in historical analysis. This is, in part, because while tools like MALLET and Gensim make it easy to apply the algorithm to a set of texts, doing so in a way that generates reasonable and reliable results is more difficult. This project sets out to use a topic model of the denomination’s periodical literature, following the suggestion of Sharon Block and David Newman’s topic model explorations of the Pennsylvania Gazette, to highlight “topic trends over time and at different resolutions” and for gaining insight on “entire publications.”17 With this approach, I am focusing on using the model to gain a broad pictures of the patterns across the texts and to identify those texts that can shed light on different aspects of the developing culture of the denomination.

The modeling algorithm returns a topic identifier for each word in the documents, an account of the most prevalent words in each topic, and a report of the prevalence of each topic in the documents of the corpus, but is agnostic as to what those topics “mean.” Standard practice is to use a topic label to summarize the language that a topic has grouped together, either by assigning it automatically from the most prevalent words in the topic or through manually assigning topic names.18 Because the language used by Seventh-day Adventist authors tends to be abstract and formulaic, methods for automatic labeling that work well in the context of scientific articles or Wikipedia proved less than informative. As a result, I relied on a human authored approach for identifying and labeling the topics.

Labeling the topics represents significant interpretive work based on close readings of the texts and the topic words. To mitigate the risk of reading too much into individual combinations of words clustered by the modeling algorithm, for each topic I read the ten to fifteen documents with the highest concentration of words assigned to that topic, and used that contextual information, together with the words of the topic, to construct the label. This method of close reading the topic results provided a more nuanced view of the pattern of word use the model had detected and helped me parse instances where similar words in the topic captured very different sets of documents. For example, topic 6 shares similar language with the “prophecy” topics that I discuss in the next section, such as the high prevalence of “daniel” and “babylon.” However, in reading the documents associated with the topic, it was apparent that the words captured by this topic were most often found in pages that contained Old Testament stories, particularly those from the historical and prophetic books such as Daniel in the Lion’s Den and the story of Esther.

Through the process of labeling the generated topics, I as the reader and interpreter bridged the gap between the model of the denominations literature created using a statistical algorithm and the models of literature created through traditional close-reading techniques. Working with set of text too large for me to read thoroughly and establish the categories of which on my own, I use the model to separate the texts into groups based on language use, use close reading of a select number of documents to understand the themes that the topic model has captured, and then use the model to get a sense of how that theme is present in the documents I have not read.

In addition, in order to more easily facilitate grouping related topics together, I created a controlled vocabulary of [x] terms. The vocabulary works to capture the major topics of the periodical literature, as separated by the topic model and identified through my evaluation, and forms the first part of the topic label. The second part of the label provides a more detailed description of the type of content within that general category. I designed this labeling scheme in order to facilitate the research goals of the project. At 250 topics, the model of the literature strikes a compromise between being generalized and being detailed. As a result, there is some overlap in topics. This provides the advantage of nuance and increases the opportunity to see shifts in language over time. However, it also makes the model more difficult to read and understand, as the fragmentation of theme over multiple topics makes is difficult to grasp broader trends. By using the labels to group topics back together, I am able to add yet another lens through which to view the corpus literature.

The labels enable readers navigate the model and provide the foundation for the work that follows in which I trace the broader picture of the prevalence of particular subjects at different times. By moving back and forth between close readings of the text and the more abstract and distant reading of the model, the reader can begin to understand and explore the overall patterns in the literature and use those patterns to identify areas for closer analysis.

[Note: This is a work in progress. Most of the current topic labels are a tentative “first draft” and are being reviewed according to the process described above.]

Identifying Expectation

In order to capture periods when Seventh-day Adventist writers and readers were focused more than usual on the second coming, I identified and traced four interrelated themes that capture the language denominational members used when speaking of the second coming and the end of time. The first theme highlights more formal explications of the key prophetic texts of Daniel and Revelations, where authors unpacked for the readers the meaning of the various figures and numbers in the biblical passages. The second contains descriptions of the second coming, where adventist writers worked to explain the events they anticipated as part of the second coming and to encourage believers to strive for the goal of heaven. The third is the parsing current and historical events in terms of their fulfillment of prophecy, or analyzing the “signs of the times.” The forth theme captures the SDA’s concern with the union of civic and religious authority. United by the idea that “Prophecy is history in advance,”19 in these themes Seventh-day Adventist authors and readers sought to understand where they stood in the temporal landscape, to verify their understanding of 1844 and their particular role in the unfolding of God’s plan, and to explain the events of the day in light of the larger trajectory of God’s plan.

In selecting these topics and organizing them into these four themes, I am offering an interpretation of the particular corpus, and Seventh-day Adventist literature in general, but also attempting to work with the strengths and limitations of the topic modeling algorithm. Topic modeling as a probabilistic algorithm, meaning that depending on where one starts, the algorithm can produce different results when run multiple times on the same corpus and even with the same parameters.20 As a result, individual words assigned to topic A in one model can be assigned to a very different topic M in another. As a result, the individual words say less than one might hope about the clustering of tokens and documents identified by the algorithm. As I discuss in the methodology, I have attempted to account for this in creating the topic labels by relying not only on the words assigned to the topic but by reading the documents where those words were drawn from. This second process of organizing topics into themes provides a second strategy for balancing the probabilistic aspect of topic modeling. When patterns repeat over a range of topics that are predominant in similar types of documents, the results are both clearer and more reliable. [plan: the effects of these different clustering decisions should be explorable through the second version of the model browser.]

Explicating Prophetic Texts

For early Seventh-day Adventist authors, the Biblical books of Daniel and Revelations offered the keys for situating themselves and their readers in time. Informed by their “rationalist” approach to the Bible, whereby they hold that all of the Bible has a clear meaning that can be understood by the faithful reader, they approach the Bible as a guidebook with clear if coded information.21 Building on a Protestant understanding of history as the linear unfolding of a divine plan that stretches from creation to the second coming, the early Seventh-day Adventists sought to identify their current position in that progression, leading up to their final salvation at Jesus’ second coming. To do so, they looked particularly to the book of Daniel to explain events of the past and to the book of Revelations to explain current events and anticipate the events to come. In these books, part of the Apocalyptic literature of the Bible, the authors look forward in time and tell of the overthrow of world powers and the eventual establishment of God’s kingdom.22 Containing visions populated with fantastical symbolic creatures, from a leopard with four wings and four heads to beasts and dragons, the authors used coded language to encourage their audience with hope of the coming fall of oppressive powers and coming days of peace.23

Seventh-day Adventist authors derived their understanding of how to interpret these text and what they represented from William Miller. Born into a religious Baptist family, Miller embraced deism in his twenties, but found himself religiously unsettled by his experiences during the War of 1812. Returning to the Baptist church, he experienced a religious conversion marked by being overwhelmed by emotions and feeling the truth and value of the Baptist narrative of salvation.24 With a faith grounded in a conversion experience, Miller turned his attention to understanding and articulating the reasonableness of that faith. Working from a set of fourteen rules, which he derived from Biblical proof texts, he developed an interpretation of the Bible, and particularly the prophetic texts, that resolved its apparent contradictions – thereby satisfying the critiques of his deist friends – and that also revealed the approximate date of the looked-for second coming: 1843.25

Charts, such as the one to the left, were used by Millerite preachers to explain to audiences how to interpret the prophecies in Daniel and Revelations. Part of the publishing and outreach efforts of Joshua V. Himes, the charts provided a visual representation of Miller’s complicated, but methodical, interpretive work. In the upper left corner, the images from Daniel are depicted and aligned to show their correlation, with the head of the statue of Daniel, chapter 2, aligned with the lion of Daniel, chapter 7, the silver chest and arms of chapter 2 with the bear of chapter 7 and the ram of chapter 8 and so forth. Across the middle, the chart bridges between the books and Daniel and Revelations through the depictions of “Pagan Rome” - the iron legs of the statue in Daniel 2, the beast of Daniel 7, and the dragon of Revelations 12. The bottom half of the chart correlates the events of history since Jesus’ death with the extended images of Revelations. All of these different elements are tied together through the dates and computations that associate the years of different historical events with the periods of time recorded in the prophetic texts.

Early Seventh-day Adventists reconciled the continuation of time after 1844 with Miller’s interpretations by arguing that Miller’s interpretation as basically correct, but that they had misunderstood the significance of October 22, 1844. While most Millerites either concluded that the dates had been miscalculated or that Miller’s whole enterprise had been misguided, a small group embraced an interpretation put forward by Hiram Edson that the “cleansing of the sanctuary” referred not to the earth as Miller had thought but marked “a new phase of Christ’s ministry in heaven that placed the earth under judgment.”26 How long this new phase would last was unknown, but believers could point to the fulfilled prophecies to know that they were indeed living in the last days.

As a result, the interpretation of Daniel and Revelations found in Millerite charts continued to play a central role to Seventh-day Adventist efforts to situate themselves temporally. Captured across three topics of the topic model, Seventh-day Adventist authors used the figures and dates of Daniel and Revelations throughout their writings to argue for their unique sense of time, to explain current events, and to anticipate events to come.

As indicated in the above charts, while descriptions of prophetic texts and the work of situating readers within the Seventh-day Adventist temporal imaginary has a continual presence within the periodical literature of the denomination, its prevalence relative to other concerns decreased over time. This is the case even when looking only at the central denominational titles, excluding the topical and regional titles that proliferated after the 1880s. This is not to say that SDA authors became less interested in or came to question the uses of these texts over time or the temporal imaginary they were used to construct. Full explications of the texts and republication of material from the 1850s can be seen well into the 20th century.27 The decline is better understood as reflecting the embrace of the SDA system for explicating the texts of Daniel and Revelations and the development of a consensus around the position of the Adventist people in sacred time. While later authors may remind their readers of the standard interpretations, they were building on existing beliefs, rather than striving to convince their readers of a new sense of time, and so required less discursive space to communicate their message.

Eschatology - Describing the Second Coming

With their roots in the belief that 1844 marked the beginning of the final events before the second coming, eschatology, or the theological study of “last things,” has a significant presence in SDA literature and in their temporal orientation. From Ellen White’s seminal work, The Great Controversy, to some of their most distinctive theological contributions, including the Sanctuary Doctrine, Conditional Immortality, and the Sabbath Doctrine (discussed in Chapter One), understanding and describing the world to come and the events leading up to it was the focus of much of the intellectual energy of the early Seventh-day Adventists.28 While most Christian groups anticipate Jesus’ return in some form, for Seventh-day Adventists that return is central to their distinctive understanding of Scripture and their self-understanding as God’s chosen people.

The topics I identified as relating to eschatology, or the study of end-times, fit into two general categories. The first set of topics, including #37, #170, and #182, offer descriptions of heaven and the experience of the second coming, using biblical passages and poetry to remind believers of the goal of the Adventist Christian life and warnings about anticipated hardships leading up to the second coming. The second set, which includes #92, #117, and #145, outlines some of the unique theological positions the denomination took with regard to the fate of the wicked and the requirements for salvation. These topics remind readers of what to expect in the days leading up to the second coming. They also provide justifications as to why events did not unfold as previously expected, using the concept of progressive revelation, or “Present Truth,” to emphasize that God reveals his plan gradually and through imperfect messengers.29

While the trajectory of these topics shows a slow decline over time in their prominence in the denominational literature, this again does not mean that these topics disappear from the denominational literature. During the first few decades of the denomination, these topics were key to establishing what would become standard Seventh-day Adventist understandings of the soul, the work of salvation, and the role of Adventists in the final events before the second coming. As these concepts became more ingrained in Adventist theology and became basic to their cultural imaginary, fewer words would have been needed to invoke these ideas for readers.

Interpreting the Signs of the Times

As a people eagerly awaiting the second coming and who believed that they could orient themselves in divine time by matching current events with events described in the Bible, denominational members closely watched news and world events. From cataloging catastrophic events and examples of government oversteps in regulating religious behavior to extended analyses of world events in light of prophecy, nearly every world event held the potential of signaling some new phase in the events leading up to the second coming. While commentators often warned readers against setting dates and reminded them that their knowledge was incomplete, the regularity of the topics served to remind readers that they were indeed living in the last days. As such, they were called on to make themselves ready and to share the Adventist message with the world.

The signs frequently mentioned by Adventist commentators range from concerns over sin and social ills to commentary on world events in light of prophecy. Spiritualism, then a prominent competitor in the religious space, and sin “as in the days of Noah” were of particular concern in the early years of the denomination (topics #26, #86). In later years, as the attention of the denomination shifted outwards, concerns about war and social unrest (topics #27, #39, #163) were the primary markers of the current point in divine time. At the turn of the century, the growing influence of Progressive reformers and those advocating for Sunday observance laws loomed particularly large in the Adventist imaginary, as signs that the anticipated collusion between the United States and the Catholic Church to enforce Sunday worship and persecute Adventists was at hand (topics #158, #242). Among the more curious “signs” are those recorded in topic #100, which captures frequent retellings of the darkening of the sun on May 19, 1780 and accounts of stars falling on November 13, 1833, some of the more supernatural-seeming events portending the second coming.30 And throughout the period, authors warned readers to anticipate unrest and persecution in the time leading up to the Jesus’ return (topic #179). World events were not just curiosities, but vital clues in tracing the unfolding of God’s plan.

Threats to the Separation of Church and State

One particular topic of concerns, and one that developed as Seventh-day Adventist began focusing more on the role of United States in the events leading up to the second coming, was the threat of the legal establishment of religion. This was a particular concern for early Seventh-day Adventists, as they had identified the first amendment and the prohibition against the establishment of religion as key aspects of the uniqueness of the United States, and the establishment of religion as the first step in the unfolding of the persecution of Adventists prior to the second coming. As resistance to the legislation of religion was understood to be one of the marks of true believers, believers tracked efforts to promote the passing of religion laws, and politically organized members to resist those efforts.

During this period of study, the most prominent movements to legislate behavior and religious practice occurred during the closing decades of the nineteenth century. Often in connection with temperance movements, Protestant religious leaders promoted what they claimed to be laws promoting general morality and social norms regarding Sunday observance. While at times these laws were drafted granting exceptions for those who designated other days for religious worship, Seventh-day Adventist leaders and others decried them as attacks on freedom of religion and the principle of religious liberty. Any attempt to exercise state power in issues of religion was the beginning of the end, both of the nation and of time, for Adventist commentators.

So important was this issue to the Adventist readership that it received a series dedicated periodical titles - Liberty, Sentinel of Liberty. In looking at the overall prevalence of the topic, these individual titles exaggerate the prevalence of the topic particularly in the years surrounding 1890. However, even when looking just at these topics in the central denominational titles, an increase in attention is visible, first around 1890 and again around 1905, in concerns about church and state.

Tracing Periods of Expectation

Examining the prevalence of all of these topics across the first seventy years of the denomination, two general features emerge. First, over time the prevalence of these topics decreases, as denominational members settle into the realization that the work of redemption was going to require much more time than had been anticipated by early church leaders in 1850. The reflects on the one hand a “naturalizing” of the discourses of end times, as the understanding of end times events and the role of the Seventh-day Adventist people in preparing for Jesus’ second coming entered into the realm of the “known” or the imaginary of the denomination. On the other hand, the decline also reflects a lengthening of the temporal imaginary, as the work facing denomination members - to reach the world with the third angel’s message - was a large undertaking that would require both time and significant effort on the part of members. [I think I have something from Bull here about how, with the death of EGW, the denomination settled in for the long haul (and turned more conservative).]

While the overall trajectory is one of decline, charting the prevalence of end-times topics also suggests four general periods of end-times expectation and readjustment over the first 70 years of the denominations history. The first, and the clearest, wave of expectation stretches from the start of the Seventh-day Adventist publishing endeavors in 1849 and reaches until approximately 1858. The second series of spikes starts around 1868 and reaches about 1875. The third, seen both across all titles and just the denominational titles, stretches from around 1886 to 1898. And the final period of unrest appears at the end of this study, starting around 1910.

This pattern fits with, while also expands, the secondary literature on the development of the denomination. In Seeking a Sanctuary, authors Bull and Lockhart note that the Seventh-day Adventist community has historically tended to be relatively quiet about end-times during periods of disruption, such as war, while instead active in periods prior or following.31 This pattern matches that captured by the topic model, as periods of heightened discourse occur in the years following the civil war, and the years leading up to the first World War. While the authors note this pattern as a curiosity, the pattern makes sense given the particular attention to the union of church and state power as the key marker of the start of the final days, and their self-understanding as the faithful remnant who would be persecuted at the end. Periods of war and conflict, while distressing and a sign of things to come, were not conducive to the type of global unification and establishment of religion that would mark the final confrontation.

Adventist theologian Jon Paulien has identified over twenty attempts to predict the date of the second coming over the history of Seventh-day Adventism, from 1844 to the 1990. Among these were repeated predictions between 1844 and 1851, a series of predictions between 1884 and 1894, and again in light of the events of World War I. While he notes that Ellen White herself repeatedly discouraged the setting of dates, for a significant percentage of believers, during these periods word events and biblical interpretation seemed to line up in such a way to suggest that the time was at hand.32 These peaks in Adventist attempts to name the date of the second coming again matches the general pattern of the model, with the model showing an additional spike in the years around 1870. This corroboration between the secondary literature and the model suggests that the model is indeed capturing and coherently classifying the linguistic features of the denominations periodical literature and that the topics I have isolated are productively showing those trends.

In the sections that follow, I will examine each of these four periods of expectation and realignment. Each section will explore the primary concerns that indicated that the second coming was at hand, and the cultural shifts that took place as Adventist believers adjusted their beliefs and expectations to explain why time continued and what their particularly mission was in the days to come.

item.title: The Emergence of Seventh-day Adventism
item.dc:creator: Jeri E. Wieringa
item.description:
I told the view to our little band in Portland, who then fully believed it to be of God. It was a powerful time. The solemnity of eternity rested upon us. About one week after this the Lord gave me another view, and shewed me the trials I must pass through, and that I must go and relate to others what he had revealed to me, and that I should meet with great opposition, and suffer anguish of spirit by going. But said the angel “The grace of God is sufficient for you: he will hold you up.”

Ellen White, 18511

And it shall come to pass afterward, that I will pour out my spirit upon all flesh; and your sons and your daughters shall prophesy, your old men shall dream dreams, your young men shall see visions

Joel 2:28, King James Version

[chapter abstract]

Setting the Stage: Women and the Revivals of the Early Republic

“Given Joel’s prophecy, the sight of a woman standing in the pulpit had cosmic significance: she was a living symbol of the last days, a reminder that the end of the world had truly come.”2

“Like earlier nineteenth-century female preachers, Millerite women solved the ‘problem’ of their gender by arguing that God had transformed their weakness into strength.”3

“Despite their desire to recapture the spirit of the earlier revivals, the Millerite’s were not identical to the sectarians of the 1810s and 1820s. Socially, they drew their membership from a higher economic class, and theologically, they placed almost as much emphasis on education as divine inspiration. Even though they did not require lecturers to be college-educated, they expected them to be able to interpret Miller’s intricate prophetic charts. At a minimum, preachers were supposed to have mastered the books of Daniel and Revelation. Reflecting the larger constituency of the movement, most Millerite female preachers seem to have been better educated than their predecessors, and they were also economically more secure.”4

“In contrast to earlier Freewill Baptists, Christians, and Methodists, the Millerites argued that married women, not single women, were best suited for careers in the pulpit. By claiming to speak as their husbands’ helpmates, female preachers tried to counter accusations that they were promiscuous, shameless, or”masculine.“5

The Making of the Adventists

Question to self: was the movement strongest in upstate New York? (claim by Brekus but unclearly supported.)

The Religious Roots of Adventism

William Miller, Joshua Himes, and ….

“Even though earlier evangelicals had realized the potential of the press, the Millerites published tracts, memoirs, and newspapers on a scale never before imagined.”6

Of the varied religious movements that developed during the nineteenth-century, one of the more notable were the Millerites, American Protestants drawn largely from Baptist and Methodist congregations who were convinced by the teaching of one William Miller that the Bible revealed that the second coming, or second advent, would take place around the year 1843. Miller, a commissioned militia officer during the War of 1812 and if his biographer is to be believed, a leading citizen of Poultney, Vermont, began his study of the Bible shortly after his conversion from Deism in an attempt to prove the reliability of the Bible by reconciling all apparent inconsistencies he discovered.7 In 1818, he first came to the conclusion that the prophecies, particularly Daniel, revealed that the second coming would take place around year 1843. After spending five years confirming his interpretations and calculation, he began to share his conclusions, starting with family and friends, then reaching out to local ministers. Miller understood his findings as reinforcing the teachings of the churches and as part of the prevailing belief in the second coming and the need for salvation. He slowly began to receive invitations to preach in a variety of churches, including Baptist, Methodist, and Congregational.8 In 1832, he published his findings in the Vermont Telegraph and in 1833, he was granted a preaching license from his Baptist church in Hampton, New York.9 He began preaching and lecturing in churches throughout New England throughout the 1830s and into the 1840s. He published a 64 page pamphlet of his interpretation in 1834 and a series of sixteen lectures in 1836. Between 1834 and 1839, when he began to with Joshua Himes, Miller recorded that he had given about 800 lectures on his interpretation of prophecy and his belief that the time of the second coming was at hand.10

Despite publishing, traveling, and preaching widely, Miller’s teachings would have remained one of many little known local religious movements of the nineteenth century if it were not for Joshua V. Himes. Prior to meeting Miller, Himes had a long history of embracing reform movements as the way to bring about the kingdom of God. Licensed to preach by the Christian Church, he was pastor of a church in Boston, was a Temperance lecturer, started a school for boys, was on the board of the Massachusetts Anti-Slavery Society, was an early supporter of William Lloyd Garrison, and distributed periodicals and other printed materials of the Disciples of Christ.11 Anticipating the coming millennium and already working hard to bring it about, Himes found Miller’s teaching that it would arrive in a mere four years time both striking and deeply motivating. With Miller’s blessing, Himes became his chief publicist, launching a campaign of print and conferences aimed at disseminating Miller’s work as quickly and widely as possible.12 Publishing periodicals such as Signs of the Times, The Midnight Cry, the Philadelphia Alarm, and The Western Midnight Cry, among others, as newspapers of the movement, along with Miller’s The Second Advent and memoirs, as well as tracts, hymns, and prophetic charts, Himes flooded religious readers with material expounding Miller’s teachings. In doing so, he fostered a sense of religious community among adventist believers and created the mechanisms by which Miller’s message could spread.13

At the risk of projecting a modern concept onto the past, it is clear that Himes had an excellent sense of “marketing” — he knew how to engage people in a cause and how to gain, if not converts, at least attention. He worked to ensure the widest possible reach for Miller’s teachings, establishing periodicals in the key cities of Boston, New York, Philadelphia, and Cincinnati. He also understood the value of “showmanship,” acting quickly on a decision to build a “great tent” — one that seated 4,000 people and was one of the largest to be seen in America; publishing and selling colorful charts to illustrate the intricate (and obtuse) details of Miller’s interpretation; and convincing Miller to offer a more definitive date. He also began holding regular conference meetings for those convinced by Miller’s teachings. These gatherings provided a forum for the dispersed community to come together, to work to reach consensus on some of the contested details of Miller’s teaching, and to agree on a strategy for spreading the word.14

Figure 1.1: William Miller’s “Chronological Chart of the World to which is added, a Chart of Daniel’s Visions” (1842). From the Adventist Digital Library. https://adventistdigitallibrary.org/adl-421835/chronological-chart-world. Accessed 6 September 2017.

Figure 1.2: Charles Fitch’s “A Chronological Chart of the Visions of Daniel and John.” (1843). From the Adventist Digital Library. https://adventistdigitallibrary.org/adl-421834/chronological-chart-visions-daniel-and-john. Accessed 6 September 2017.

The efforts of Himes launched Miller and his teachings into the public consciousness and created a community around the belief that the second coming would occur between March 21, 1843, and March 21, 1844. In 1842, just two years after he joined the cause, Himes claimed fifty-thousand readers for Signs of the Times and between three and four hundred ministers distributing the materials.15 By 1844, Himes had overseen the foundation of a number of serial publications, tracts, and pamphlets and had organized, attended, and spoken at conferences around the United States and Canada. As a result, Miller himself became highly sought-after speaker, claiming to have given about 4000 lectures in 500 hundred towns between 1840 and 1844. In addition to Miller and Himes, by Miller’s calculations some 200 ministers in the United States and Canada had embraced his interpretation, and an additional 500 public lecturers circulated his view.16

Miller did not set out to form a new movement or denomination. Rather he saw his teachings as within the bounds of the prevailing orthodoxy, as the logical conclusion of prevailing Protestant beliefs. He made no effort to start his own church and did not wish to be identified as a “sectarian leader,” instead encouraging followers to stay within their home denominations. In claiming success, he notes that, as result of his early lecturing, “many churches thereby greatly added to their numbers,” a statement that reinforces that he saw his goal as the revival of the local church, not the creation of his own.17 He saw his teaching of the imminent second coming to be a truth of general interest for all denominations, and one that would (or should) be embraced regardless of denominational affiliation.18

This did not always go according to plan, as the experience of the Harmon family illustrates. In her autobiography, Ellen (Harmon) White reports, “At the age of eleven I was converted, and when twelve years old was baptized, and joined the Methodist church.” Upon hearing William Miller lecture on the topic of the Second Advent at age of 13 (1841), she “then felt that I was not holy, not ready to see Jesus” and so “when the invitation was given for church members and sinners to come forward for prayer,” she went forward in the belief that “I must have a great work done for me to fit me for Heaven.”19 Although already converted, baptized, and a member of the church, the news that the second coming would occur in two years time caused White to call her faith into question. She began regularly attending “Second Advent meetings,” seeking “full and free salvation” from God.20 She received the confirmation she sought when she obeyed God’s prompting to “pray in a public prayer-meeting.”21

Convinced of her salvation and full of anticipation for the return of Jesus, she returned to her Methodist class-meeting some six months later to share “what Jesus had done for me, and what a fullness I enjoyed through believing that the Lord was coming.” This message, however, was not acceptable to the local Methodist class-leader, whom she reports interrupted her testimony to add “Through Methodism,” an addition she rejected because “it was Christ and the hope of his soon coming that had made me free.”22 Eventually the tensions between Harmon family and the local Methodist minister over their Millerite convictions became too great and the family was “at one time cast out of the Methodist Church.”23

Local communities of adventist believers emphasized regular attendance at the local Protestant Sunday services, but also attended their own interdenominational meetings of those who believed the second coming was at hand. Dedicated to sharing the news of the second coming with their neighbors and religious fellows, members of Millerite associations often found themselves at odds with their local religious leaders.24 Finding community among other adventists and meeting resistance in their local churches was often too much for individual believers, prompting them to leave their home denominations and claim an adventist identify. While Miller himself was quite distressed by this trend, it set the stage for new denominations to form in the wake of the disappointments of 1844.25

Because of the non-denominational aspects of Miller’s preaching and because multiple dates were eventually given for the second Advent, the total number of people who joined Miller in anticipating the second coming and the end of the world is difficult to determine. Miller estimated that there were 200 ministers and 500 lecturers who were had embraced his teachings. In the years after the 1844, the New York Tribune estimated that there were 30-40,000 Millerites at the movements peak. The high end of estimates puts the peak number at 100,000, though Miller himself claimed that about 50,000 embraced his message, calculating based on the number of conversions he witnessed in his lectures.26 These were the believers — those who embraced Miller’s interpretation as, quite literally, gospel truth. Given the massive amount of literature produced by Himes, however, it is likely that many more quietly marked the passage of 1844 with interested skepticism. What is clear is that, although Miller was able to preach to nearly 500,000 people, what propelled his teaching from local anticipation to an international movement was the coordinated publishing efforts of Himes.27

As would be the case for the early Seventh-day Adventists, Himes recognized the power of print and effectively deployed it as the center around which the Millerite movement formed. Regular publications spread the content of Miller’s interpretation, raising awareness of his findings. Those same publications provided the forum by which Himes organized the regular conferences, inviting interested people to gather together to coordinate their efforts to spread the news of the coming millennium, and advertised upcoming tent meetings. Reports about the successes of the camp meetings helped the community to take part in the events regardless of geographic proximity, and served as further proof of the truth and successfulness of the adventist message, for if God were not behind the movement, the events would not be successful. In addition, Himes strategically started multiple publications in different cultural and geographic centers on the U.S., increasing the coverage that the movement could achieve and catering to regional interests. This was a strategy that the Seventh-day Adventists would later emulate, first as they came together around the publication of a new interpretation of Miller’s teachings and the events of 1844, and later as they sent out missionaries, establishing printing houses in each new geographic region they entered.

Becoming Seventh-day Adventists

The Fracturing of the Adventists

“The Albany Conference represented the beginning of the Adventist Christian Church, a new denomination with its own distinct beliefs and rituals. … Replacing the flexibility of their earlier churches with greater structure and discipline, they discouraged visionary enthusiasm, established a professional clergy, and forbade women to serve as evangelists.”28

As the period Miller identified between March 21, 1843 and March 21, 1844, passed, adventist believers began to develop a number of alternative theories to address the persistence of time. A temporary reprieve from the crisis caused by persistence of time was granted when a young man named Samuel Snow announced that he had identified the error in Miller’s calculations and that October 22, 1844, was the correct date indicated for the second coming. While acceptance of that interpretation brought unity back to the movement for a time, with the passing of the October 22, which came to be known as the Great Disappointment, the tensions between the various groups of adventists became too great to maintain a unified movement.

The adventist community did not collapse immediately after the final disappointment of October 22, 1844. While Himes briefly suspended publication after the October 16 issue of The Advent Herald and Signs of the Times Reporter, in anticipation of the second coming, when the day passed without event, he quickly regathered, releasing a new issue on October 30, 1844. Still convinced of the truth of the core of the adventist message, that the time of the second coming was at hand, he offered a retelling of the history of the adventist movement that emphasized the nuances of their teachings around the date of the second coming and downplayed the significance of the October date.29 However, understanding and explaining the persistence of time posed a significant challenge for the community.

Many of those who had joined the adventist cause leading up to the October date returned to their original religious homes, joined other movements, such as the Shakers, or left the faith all together. Among those who remained committed to Miller’s teachings, the movement split into two main groups: those who held that the end was indeed near but they had been mistaken about the date; and those who held that the end was indeed near but that they had been mistaken about the significance of the date. The debates between these groups took place on the pages of the main adventist papers, as well as in the pages of new periodicals started to promote various interpretations of the nature and timing of the Second Advent.30 While Miller himself continued to believe that his interpretation was correct and the second coming was at hand, he ceased to offer or support any definitive date predictions after 1844.31

Those who would come to form Seventh-day Adventism were part of the second category of movements to come out of adventism, believing that Miller had been correct in his interpretation of the Bible, and his endorsement of October 22, 1844, as the date prophesied but incorrect about what that date signified.32 They embraced what were considered some of the more radical theological positions discussed in the wake of the 1844. First, they embraced the teaching of “conditional immortality,” viewing the standard teaching of an immortal soul to be extra-biblical, arguing instead that people would be granted immortality (or not) at the resurrection. Second, this group of Adventists embraced the Seventh-day Baptist position on keeping Saturday, rather than Sunday, as the Sabbath. Third, rather than question the date Miller and Snow had given for the second coming, the founders of Seventh-day Adventism questioned the event that the date marked, holding what became known as the Sanctuary Doctrine. This was the belief that October 22, 1844, marked the beginning of Christ’s work cleansing the sanctuary, which was “heavenly,” rather than being the earth as Miller had assumed, and there Jesus was undertaking the work of “blotting out sins” ahead of his second coming. Fourth, they embraced the existence of prophetic gifts, the belief that God would speak directly through an individual to provide guidance and new revelation for a community. For the early Seventh-day Adventists, this gift was primarily limited to Ellen (Harmon) White, though early on a number of people claimed to have received visions. Finally, although this was eventually abandoned, they embraced the “shut door” doctrine, holding that October 22, 1844, marked a closing of the period of salvation and only those who had accepted adventism prior to the date could be saved.33 As with others who continued in the Adventist faith after 1844, all of these beliefs hinged on a core belief that the waiting time they were now in would be short and that the second coming would take place soon.

Developing a Distinctive Theology

Living at the End of Time

“Although White, Mussey, and Wellcome managed to preserve the Millerite legacy of female evangelism, they moved in increasingly conservative directions during the 1850s and 1860s.”34

“According to Beulah Matthewson, who published an article and a book defending female preaching, women could speak as men’s helpmates, but they certainly could not be ordained. Even though they could pray aloud, sing, witness, exhort, or preach, they were forbidden to”assume the leadership," or rob men of their rightful authority in the home and the church. … Until history came to an end, they would have to humbly accept their subordination to men.“35

item.title: Constructing Computational Models from Historical Texts: A Consideration of Methods
item.dc:creator: Jeri E. Wieringa
item.description:
My goal in this dissertation is to to identify periods of millennial expectation in the development of Seventh-day Adventism, and show the effects of those periods on the culture of the religious movement using the particular computational method of topic modeling. To that end, there are three methodological aspects of this project that require more detailed discussion. The first is my selection of a corpus that can illuminate broad patterns across the denomination. The second is my approach to processing that corpus in preparation for computational analysis, and the ways choices made during text preparation shape the analysis. And the third is my selection and use of a topic modeling algorithm that both fits the textual data at hand and can help illuminate overall patterns in language and concerns of the denomination.

The discussion of methods, such as what follows here, and a commitment to reproducible code, provide the context necessary to evaluate research based on computational analysis. One persistent critique of arguments based on computational analysis is that it is difficult to assess the soundness of arguments. Even between projects that use similar modes of computational analysis, variations in corpus selection and processing can lead to conclusions that are difficult to compare, and it can be unclear which application is more reliable than others. Some of that difficulty can be addressed by discussing the methodological aspects of the project, such as the match between sources and question, the applicability of modeling algorithm to the questions at hand, the application of the algorithm to the data, and the evaluation of the model. Additionally, executing and documenting code in ways that can be reproduced by others exposes the implicit and explicit assumptions enacted in the code open to evaluation and critique. By describing my sources, computational approach, and methods of interpretation, I am providing the means by which the project can be verified and assessed similar to how footnotes and discussions of research methods support the verification and assessment of historical research presented in monograph form.

Developing a Corpus for A Gospel of Health and Salvation

In order to identify significant and meaningful patterns in the development of the religious culture of Seventh-day Adventism, this project requires an appropriate set of sources to abstract from, both in terms of format and content. Here the Seventh-day Adventist church offers a number of advantages for undertaking the sort of overall analysis that I have proposed. Central to that endeavor has been the work of the Ellen G. White Estate, which has labored since Ellen White’s death in 1915 to share her writings with all interested readers. In carrying out their mission, the directors and staff of the Estate have regularly embraced new technologies as they have become available. While the estate has focused on indexing, republishing, and digitizing White’s published and unpublished writings, the denomination has also embraced efforts to make their history more readily available. Supported by local interest in new technologies and the publishing mission of the denomination, the denomination has undertaken an extensive (and unique in scale) effort to scan, OCR, and make publicly available the literature of the denomination.1

The titles available online - accessed through the Office of Archives, Statistics, and Research and more recently through the Adventist Digital Library - privilege the bureaucratic documents of the denomination, including statistical documents, minutes and reports, and the periodical and tract literature of the denomination. The most extensive collection of documents available are the denominational periodicals. While the collection privileges the centrally produced titles, overall it provides access to a range of the periodical literature produced by the denomination.2

Periodicals played a key role in the development of the religious culture of early Seventh-day Adventism, and as such provide content well-suited to the intellectual question at hand. While most nineteenth-century religious denominations utilized print to connect their members, as a medium for evangelism, and as a forum for articulating theological differences, periodical literature played a particularly important role in the development of early Seventh-day Adventism.3 It was to periodicals that Ellen and James White first turned in their work to unite the adventists in the years after Miller’s failed millennial prediction of October 21, 1844.4 The choice of medium was defended in 1850, when Ellen reported that she was shown in a vision that God was seeking to bring his people together around the truth of the seventh-day message, an effort that required “that the truth be published in a paper, as preached.”5

In addition to being the medium of communication through which the nascent Seventh-day Adventist community began to organize and work out their theological positions, the publications also functioned as the center of the movement’s “imagined community.”6 While the first two issues The Present Truth focused primarily on arguments for Saturday Sabbath-keeping and presenting Ellen White’s vision, by the third issue James White published notices of upcoming conference meetings.7 By the forth issue, White published a letter from one J.C. Bowles, who wrote from Jackson, Michigan to suggest that James “insert extract of the letters you may receive from the brethren” as it would be “comforting … to hear from others” and “may induce some to examine the subject, that would not otherwise.”8 While James notes in the same issue that he did not intend initially to publish letters from the “brethren,” such quickly became a regular feature of The Present Truth and its successor, The Second Advent Review and Sabbath Herald. By the last issue of The Present Truth (volume 1.11, published November 1850) over half of the publication was devoted to letters from readers, responses to controversies within the community, news about recent and upcoming meetings, and the like. As a large percentage of the early community were “isolated Sabbath keepers,” members who did not have a Saturday keeping church to join, and believers were dispersed throughout the northern and western states, the literature of the denomination, and predominantly its periodical literature, functioned as the “tie that binds” for the young Seventh-day Adventist community.9

The Seventh-day Adventist denomination and its publishing efforts began small, from 1000 copies of The Present Truth in published by James White in 1850, but grew quickly. In addition to growing their central publications of The Review and Herald and The Youth’s Instructor, they launched additional titles as they spread geographically, coupling missionary efforts with the establishment of new printing houses. Shortly after the denomination formally organized in 1863, the Review and Herald Publishing Association boasted 20 employees, approximate $39,000 in assets and $4000 in sales.10 By 1920, the publishing arm of the denomination employed 1,125 individuals in 45 publishing houses worldwide, produced 144 different periodical titles and literature in 99 languages, with assets valued over 3 million dollars and annual sales amounts over 5.6 million dollars.11

In addition, the denominational members produced numerous books, including theological treatises and testimonials, tracts, and study guides, along with hymnals and cookbooks. This publication empire supported, and was supported by, the labor of church members and missionaries as “colporteurs,” or book peddlers, a role that enabled lay members to contribute to the mission of the church while also supporting themselves in other church-related activities, such as school attendance.12 The literature produced by the denomination was also in conversation with a range of nineteenth-century materials produced by reformers of diet, medical care, and the home, particularly Sylvester Graham, William Alcott, Russel Trall, James Caleb Jackson, and Catharine Beecher.13 The universe of published literature connected to the development of Seventh-day Adventism is quite large, as the denomination developed within the nexus of American reform movements and the religious revivalism of the nineteenth century.

I focused my study on the periodical literature produced from four geographic regions within the United States: the Great Lakes (organized within the denomination as the Lake Union Conference), the West Coast (Pacific Union Conference), the Mid-Atlantic (Columbia Union Conference), and the Southern Mississippi River Valley (Southern Union Conference). These four regions were home to the major publishing and health reform centers of the denomination, and were sites of missionary activity as well as some contention over the leadership of the denomination. Focusing on these four regions also provides a useful balance between two of the largest regions of the SDA (Lake Union and Pacific Union) and two of the smaller regions (Columbia Union and Southern Union).

Using the boundaries of the regions as defined by the denomination in 1920, my initial research step was to gather the publications that were produced predominantly within these four regions which have been digitized by the denomination. Because this is a specialized collection of literature, only a few of the titles have been digitized as part of large digitization projects, such as HathiTrust, and while a few titles are included in the Historical Periodicals Collection produced by the American Antiquarian Society, the most extensive and easiest to access collection of the periodicals has been produced by the denomination itself.14

Limiting my selection to periodicals published from within the above four regional conferences and digitized by the Seventh-day Adventist denomination, I gathered a corpus composed of 30 different periodical titles, of which there were 13,340 issues and 197,943 pages of material. For a full list of the 30 titles included in this study, see Table 2.2. This scale of materials is important, as it enables me to pursue a richer understanding of Adventist discourse than I could achieve were I to rely on one or two titles alone. But it also requires both the historian and the reader to approach the materials differently, to rely on computational tools to identify areas of interest and to surface general patterns in the discourse of the denomination, with an awareness of the strengths and limitations of both the data and the methods.

The largest periodicals in my study are the four centrally produced denominational titles — the Review and Herald (RH), the Youth’s Instructor (YI), Signs of the Times (ST), and the Health Reformer (HR). In these titles, the leaders of the denomination sought to guide the beliefs and practices of the denomination, publishing pieces on theology, health, and the everyday life of Seventh-day Adventists. Also through these publications, community members responded back to the leadership through letters and submissions of their own. The corpus contains twice as many pages of the largest title, the Review and Herald, than of the next most significant contributor, the Health Reformer. Together, the Review and Herald, Youth’s Instructor and Signs of the Times, plus the General Conference Bulletin, The Present Truth and Advent Review constitute half of the entire corpus, weighting the dataset heavily toward the centrally produced publications of the denomination.

However, relying on the central publications of the denomination would provide only a partial picture of the diversity of thought and practice within the denomination. While vital to understanding development of an institution over time, the viewpoints expressed in these publications privilege the official position of the denomination. Covering a number of topical and regional focuses, including education, health, missions, and “religious liberty,” the other half of my corpus offers a different range of voices.15 Many of the newly-formed regional and area conferences began producing their own periodicals in the early 20th century as a way to connect the local community, as well as to report back to the international denomination. These regional publications, although often short-lived, provide colloquial information on the activities of the denomination, featured reports from the local conferences, letters, and updates on the activities of the conference, particularly with regards to selling denominational literature.

The proliferation of topical and regional publications also created challenges for denominational leaders, particularly when the viewpoints presented came into conflict with the official position of the denomination. Traces of these contests can be seen in the remaining archival record, as the efforts to shape and control the denomination’s message continues into the present. A useful example of this can be seen in the digitization and distribution of the denomination’s health periodicals. The Health Reformer was one of the early publications started by James and Ellen White, and was the first new publication launched after the denomination organized in 1863. By 1875, John Harvey Kellogg had taken the lead as the principal editor of the publication and his control over the publication was such that the publication closely mirrors the developments of Kellogg’s own understanding of health as it changed over time. In 1907, Kellogg was disfellowshipped by the denomination, though he retained control over the publication of the Health Reformer and continued its publication well into the 20th century. The archivists and digitization teams at the Seventh-day Adventist church, however, did not include any issues of the Health Reformer (later known as Good Health) after 1907, an archival enactment of denominational politics and reflective of the fact after 1907, Kellogg was no longer considered to be a voice of the denomination. Rather, Life and Health, which was published out of Washington, D.C., became the central publication for the denomination’s health message, one that was under closer control by the religious leaders of the church than the Health Reformer ever was.
